items.stem: Which period of English is roughly dated 1500–1800?
items.answer: Early Modern English

items.stem: Explain the significance of Samuel Johnson’s A Dictionary of the English Language (1755) in the history of English.
items.answer: It gave English an authoritative reference for spelling and meaning.

items.stem: Explain the significance of the expansion of the British Empire (the 18th–19th centuries) in the history of English.
items.answer: It brought borrowings from many languages, e.g. bungalow and pyjamas from Hindi/Urdu.

items.stem: Read a letter from a London merchant to his brother (1665): ‘Deare Brother, I received yours of the 3d instant, and am glad to heare that thou and thy Family are in good Health. The Sicknesse encreaseth here dayly, so that I doe purpose to remove my Wife and Children into the Countrey. Trade is very dead, and no Ship hath come into the River this fortnight. I pray thee send me word whether the Wooll be sold, and at what price. Thy loving Brother, Thomas’ Identify two features of Early Modern English in this text and explain how each differs from present-day English.
items.answer: ‘Deare Brother’ – non-standard (pre-dictionary) spelling: final -e (‘Deare’, ‘heare’) reflects variable spelling before standardisation. ‘thou and thy Family’ – archaic second-person pronoun: ‘thou/thy’ is used between close family, marking intimacy (the T/V distinction).
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘Deare Brother’ (non-standard (pre-dictionary) spelling): final -e (‘Deare’, ‘heare’) reflects variable spelling before standardisation; ‘thou and thy Family’ (archaic second-person pronoun): ‘thou/thy’ is used between close family, marking intimacy (the T/V distinction); ‘The Sicknesse encreaseth here dayly’ (-eth third-person verb inflection): ‘encreaseth’ shows the older -eth ending, later replaced by -s; ‘I doe purpose’ (auxiliary do in a positive statement): unstressed periphrastic ‘do’ in a statement, common in EME, now used only for emphasis; ‘no Ship hath come’ (archaic verb form): ‘hath’ is the older third-person form of ‘have’; ‘my Wife and Children into the Countrey’ (capitalisation of common nouns): common nouns are capitalised, a printing and writing convention that declined in the late 18th century; ‘I pray thee send me word’ (politeness formula): ‘I pray thee’ is an archaic request formula, now replaced by ‘please’; ‘yours of the 3d instant’ (archaic lexis): ‘instant’ means ‘of this month’, a business convention now largely obsolete.

items.stem: Read an advertisement from a newspaper (1752): ‘To be SOLD, at the Golden Lion in Cheapſide, a large Parcel of the fineſt Tea, Coffee and Chocolate, lately imported, at reaſonable Rates. Likewiſe a choice Collection of Muſick for the Harpſichord. N.B. Ladies and Gentlemen may be ſupplied at their own Houſes. Thoſe who pleaſe to favour him with their Commands may depend upon being ſerved with the utmoſt Care and Diſpatch.’ Identify four features of Early Modern English in this text and explain how each differs from present-day English.
items.answer: ‘Cheapſide’ – long s (ſ): the long s was used in non-final positions in print until about 1800. ‘Muſick’ – non-standard (pre-dictionary) spelling: ‘Musick’ keeps the -ck ending that Johnson retained but which later lost the k. ‘a large Parcel of the fineſt Tea, Coffee and Chocolate’ – capitalisation of common nouns: nouns such as ‘Parcel’, ‘Tea’ are capitalised. ‘lately imported’ – archaic lexis: ‘lately’ for ‘recently’ is now rare in this sense.
items.markingKey: Award up to 5 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘Cheapſide’ (long s (ſ)): the long s was used in non-final positions in print until about 1800; ‘Muſick’ (non-standard (pre-dictionary) spelling): ‘Musick’ keeps the -ck ending that Johnson retained but which later lost the k; ‘a large Parcel of the fineſt Tea, Coffee and Chocolate’ (capitalisation of common nouns): nouns such as ‘Parcel’, ‘Tea’ are capitalised; ‘lately imported’ (archaic lexis): ‘lately’ for ‘recently’ is now rare in this sense; ‘Thoſe who pleaſe to favour him with their Commands’ (politeness formula): deferential, elaborate phrasing typical of 18th-century commerce; ‘N.B.’ (Latin abbreviation): ‘nota bene’ reflects the prestige of Latin in written English; ‘To be SOLD’ (graphological emphasis): capitals in print draw attention, as in modern adverts.

items.stem: Read an entry from a traveller’s journal (1790): ‘We set out betimes, the Road being exceeding bad by reason of the late Rains. The Coachman, a surly Fellow, would not be perswaded to drive faster than a Walk, whereat my Companion was much vexed. About Noon we reached an Inn, where we dined very indifferently upon a Fowl that had seen better Days. ’Tis a pity the Country is so ill provided with good Roads, for the Prospect is uncommon fine.’ Analyse ways in which this text exemplifies the characteristics of English of its period. Refer to specific details from the text.
items.answer: Indicative content: ‘We set out betimes’ (archaic lexis): ‘betimes’ (early) has fallen out of use; ‘exceeding bad’ (adjective used as an adverb intensifier): ‘exceeding’ without -ly as an intensifier, now non-standard; ‘would not be perswaded’ (non-standard (pre-dictionary) spelling): ‘perswaded’ is an older spelling of ‘persuaded’; ‘whereat my Companion was much vexed’ (archaic lexis): ‘whereat’ (at which) and ‘vexed’ (annoyed) are now formal or archaic; ‘’Tis a pity’ (archaic contraction): ‘’Tis’ (it is) is a contraction now found only in poetry or archaism; ‘uncommon fine’ (adjective used as an adverb intensifier): ‘uncommon’ for ‘uncommonly’; ‘dined very indifferently’ (semantic change): ‘indifferently’ here means ‘poorly’, a sense now less common; ‘the Road being exceeding bad’ (capitalisation of common nouns): ‘Road’, ‘Rains’, ‘Coachman’ are capitalised, though the practice was declining by 1790; context: 1790, before/after standardisation; modern version: We set out early, because the road was extremely bad after the recent rain. The coachman, a grumpy man, could not be persuaded to go faster than walking pace, which annoyed my companion …

The coachman, a grumpy man, could not be persuaded to go faster than walking pace, which annoyed my companion …

items.stem: What is semantic broadening?
options: A word’s meaning becoming more general over time
A word’s meaning becoming more specific
items.answer: A word’s meaning becoming more general over time
items.markingKey: E.g. holiday: holy day → any day off.

items.stem: Explain how the word ‘cardigan’ was formed and suggest one reason why such words enter the language.
items.answer: Eponym: named after the Earl of Cardigan.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 per valid point: identifies the process (eponym); explains the formation (named after the Earl of Cardigan); a plausible cause, e.g. the need for euphemism.

items.answer: Acronym: North Atlantic Treaty Organization, pronounced as a word.

items.stem: Felix has collected these words while investigating lexical change: ‘pretty’, ‘URL’, ‘emoticon’. For each word, identify the process of lexical or semantic change and explain how it applies.
items.answer: ‘pretty’: amelioration (once ‘cunning’ or ‘crafty’; now ‘attractive’). ‘URL’: initialism (uniform resource locator, letters pronounced separately). ‘emoticon’: blending (emotion + icon).
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘pretty’ – amelioration: once ‘cunning’ or ‘crafty’; now ‘attractive’; ‘URL’ – initialism: uniform resource locator, letters pronounced separately; ‘emoticon’ – blending: emotion + icon.

items.stem: Omar has collected these words while investigating lexical change: ‘a must’, ‘deer’, ‘to edit’, ‘pyjamas’. For each word, identify the process of lexical or semantic change and explain how it applies.
items.answer: ‘a must’: conversion (the modal ‘must’ used as a noun). ‘deer’: narrowing (once any animal; now a particular animal). ‘to edit’: back-formation (formed by removing -or from editor). ‘pyjamas’: borrowing (from Hindi/Urdu).
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘a must’ – conversion: the modal ‘must’ used as a noun; ‘deer’ – narrowing: once any animal; now a particular animal; ‘to edit’ – back-formation: formed by removing -or from editor; ‘pyjamas’ – borrowing: from Hindi/Urdu.

items.stem: The following words have entered English in the 21st century: ‘vlog’, ‘to livestream’, ‘staycation’. Analyse how each was formed and evaluate what these words suggest about the causes of lexical change today.
items.answer: ‘vlog’: blending/clipping (video + blog). ‘to livestream’: compounding and conversion (live + stream, used as a verb). ‘staycation’: blending (stay + vacation). They reflect technology, social media and changing social practices.
items.markingKey: Award up to 4 marks, 1 per valid point: ‘vlog’: blending/clipping (video + blog); ‘to livestream’: compounding and conversion (live + stream, used as a verb); ‘staycation’: blending (stay + vacation); causes: technology and the internet; causes: social and cultural change; evaluation, e.g. speed of spread through social media; some words may not last.

items.stem: When was Samuel Johnson’s A Dictionary of the English Language published?
items.markingKey: Johnson’s dictionary (1755) became the standard authority for spelling for over a century.

items.stem: Explain how the printing press contributed to standardisation.
items.answer: Printing spread a single written variety widely and encouraged consistent spellings.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 per valid point: mass production of identical texts; spread of the London/south-east Midlands variety; printers’ house styles fixed spellings; some spellings fixed before the Great Vowel Shift ended, so spelling and sound diverged.

items.stem: Explain why Johnson’s Dictionary was important in the standardisation of English.
items.answer: It codified spelling and meanings, providing an authority used by printers, schools and writers.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks, 1 per valid point: codified spelling and meaning (about 40,000 entries); used illustrative quotations from literature as authority; adopted by printers, schools and publishers; reduced variation in spelling (though not all spellings were rational).

items.stem: Read instructions from a household management book (1845): ‘The mistress of a household should rise early, for it is impossible that her servants should be punctual if she is not. The breakfast-table must be laid by eight o’clock. Let the kitchen be inspected daily, and let no waste be suffered. Whilst the lady need not herself perform menial tasks, she ought to understand them, that she may judge whether they are well done.’ Rewrite the first two sentences in present-day standard English, and explain two of the orthographic or grammatical changes you made.
items.answer: Model: Householders should get up early: staff will not be punctual otherwise. Breakfast must be laid by eight. Check the kitchen every day and do not allow waste … Changes: modal verb of obligation (‘should rise early’); let + passive imperative (‘Let the kitchen be inspected daily’).
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks, 1 per valid point: accurate modernisation; ‘should rise early’: modal verb of obligation – deontic modals (should, must, ought to) give advice with moral authority; ‘Let the kitchen be inspected daily’: let + passive imperative – an indirect, impersonal command structure now rare; ‘let no waste be suffered’: semantic change – ‘suffered’ means ‘allowed’, a sense now archaic; ‘Whilst the lady’: conjunction now declining – ‘whilst’ is declining in frequency in favour of ‘while’; ‘that she may judge’: subjunctive / archaic purpose clause – ‘that she may’ for ‘so that she can’ is now formal; ‘breakfast-table’: hyphenated compound – compounds often begin hyphenated and later close up or open (‘breakfast table’); ‘her servants’: social context – reference to servants reflects the class structure of Victorian households.

items.stem: What does an n-gram viewer graph usually show?
options: The relative frequency of a word or phrase in a large corpus over time
The meaning of a word in each year
The number of speakers of English
items.answer: The relative frequency of a word or phrase in a large corpus over time
items.markingKey: Frequency is normally given per million words (or as a percentage) by year.

items.stem: Explain two limitations of using an n-gram viewer to investigate the change from ‘e-mail’ to ‘email’.
items.answer: The corpus is mainly published writing, so informal, spoken and online usage is under-represented; OCR errors, genre bias and house styles can distort frequencies.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark, 1 per valid point: corpus is mostly published books, not speech or informal writing; OCR (scanning) errors, e.g. long s read as f; publishers’ house styles may impose spellings; genre or regional imbalance in the corpus; frequency shows use, not attitudes or meaning.

items.stem: What is a prescriptive approach to language?
options: One that sets rules for how language should be used and judges usage as correct or incorrect
One that studies only spoken language
One that studies only historical texts
One that records how language is actually used
items.answer: One that sets rules for how language should be used and judges usage as correct or incorrect
items.markingKey: Prescriptivism lays down norms; descriptivism records usage.

items.stem: This comment appeared in a radio phone-in: ‘Text-speak is an epidemic that children catch from their phones.’ Explain the attitude to language change it shows.
items.answer: Infectious disease: it describes change as a contagious illness.

items.stem: Explain why English spelling is often said to be irregular.
items.answer: Spelling was fixed by printing and dictionaries while pronunciation continued to change, and borrowings kept foreign spellings.
